notes.7:26: The Vulgate specifies ex idolo ("from an idol", vs. Hebrew "an abomination") and retains the loanword anathema, denoting something placed under a divine ban and devoted to destruction.
notes.8:3: The Vulgate reads in omni verbo quod egreditur de ore Dei ("on every word that comes out from the mouth of God"), supplying verbo ("word") and reading Dei ("of God") in agreement with the Septuagint and Matthew 4:4, whereas the Hebrew lacks "word" and uses the divine name.
notes.8:4: The Vulgate reads non est subtritus ("was not worn sore" or chafed) rather than the Hebrew "did not swell," and ends with en quadragesimus annus est ("look, it is the fortieth year") rather than "these forty years."
notes.8:15: The Vulgate renders the wilderness perils vividly as serpens flatu adurens ("the serpent scorching with its breath") and dipsas, an ancient desert viper whose bite was said to cause fatal thirst, interpreting the Hebrew word for "thirsty ground."
notes.8:16: The Vulgate reads ad extremum misertus est tui ("in the end He had mercy on you") and subordinates verse 17 directly to it as a purpose clause, whereas the Hebrew reads "to do good to you in your latter end."
notes.8:18: The Vulgate reads quod ipse vires tibi praebuerit ("that He Himself has given you strength") without the Hebrew phrase "to gain wealth," and adds indicat ("shows") in sicut praesens indicat dies.
notes.9:2: The Vulgate reads "whom you yourself have seen and heard, whom no one can resist face to face" (quos ipse vidisti et audisti, quibus nullus potest ex adverso resistere), whereas the Hebrew text reads "whom you know and of whom you have heard it said, 'Who can stand before the sons of Anak?'"
notes.9:12: The Vulgate reads "the way that you showed them" (viam, quam demonstrasti eis), referring to Moses in the second person, where the Hebrew has "the way that I commanded them" (compare 9:16, "which He had shown you").
notes.9:14: The Vulgate reads "appoint you over a nation" (constituam te super gentem) rather than the Hebrew "make you into a nation."
notes.9:22: The Vulgate translates the three Hebrew wilderness place names (Taberah, Massah, and Kibroth-hattaavah) etymologically into Latin as "the Burning" (incendium), "the Testing" (tentatio), and "the Graves of Craving" (Sepulchra concupiscentiae).
notes.10:3: Latin "de lignis setim" transliterates the Hebrew term (shittim) for acacia wood.
notes.10:15: Latin "conglutinatus est" literally means "was glued/bonded closely together with," vividly rendering the Hebrew verb for setting one's affection on someone; "as is confirmed today" (sicut hodie comprobatur) is also a distinctly Vulgate rendering of Hebrew "as at this day."
notes.10:17: Latin "Dominus dominantium" uses a participle (literally "Lord of those who rule"), corresponding to Hebrew "Lord of lords"; "shows no partiality" renders the Latin idiom "personam non accipit" (literally "does not accept a person").
notes.10:20: The Vulgate includes "alone" (ei soli, "Him alone"), agreeing with the Septuagint and the quotation in Matthew 4:10 and Luke 4:8, where the Masoretic Hebrew has simply "Him."
notes.11:7: The Vulgate connects vv. 7-8 into a single sentence with the purpose clause "ut custodiatis" ("so that you may keep"), whereas the Hebrew begins a new independent command at v. 8.
notes.11:10: Where the Hebrew refers to watering Egypt "with your foot," the Vulgate renders the clause passively as "aquæ ducuntur irriguæ" ("irrigating waters are channeled").
notes.11:14: The Vulgate uses the third person "dabit" ("He will give") rather than the Hebrew first person ("I will give"), and in v. 15 construes "fœnumque ex agris" ("and hay from the fields") as an object of "colligatis" ("gather") rather than a separate clause.
notes.11:30: Instead of transliterating the Hebrew place name "elonei Moreh" ("oaks/terebinths of Moreh"), the Vulgate renders it descriptively as "vallem tendentem et intrantem procul" ("the valley that stretches out and goes far inward").
notes.12:3: The Vulgate renders the Canaanite cult objects as "statuas" ("statues," for Hebrew pillars), "lucos" ("groves," for Hebrew Asherim), and "idola" ("idols"), and uses the plural for both "nomina" ("names") and "locis illis" ("those places").
notes.12:10: The Vulgate joins the end of v. 10 ("habitetis") directly to the ablative phrase beginning v. 11 ("in loco, quem elegerit..."), whereas the Hebrew concludes the sentence at v. 10 and opens a new clause at v. 11.
notes.12:15: The Vulgate treats "immundum" and "mundum" as neuter adjectives referring to the animal and inserts explanatory glosses ("that is, blemished and weak" and "that is, whole and without blemish, which is lawful to offer"), whereas the Hebrew refers to ceremonially unclean and clean persons eating the meat (as the Vulgate itself does with masculine forms in v. 22).
notes.12:23: Latin "pro anima" ("in place of the life," where "anima" can mean "life" or "soul") softens the Hebrew's direct identification ("the blood is the life").
notes.12:30: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew "be ensnared after them" as "imiteris eas" ("imitate them") and translates "before you" with the ablative absolute "te ... introëunte" ("as you enter").
notes.13:1: As in the Hebrew, chapter 13 begins with this verse (numbered 12:32 in some other versifications), so the rest of the chapter is numbered one higher. Latin "do this alone for the Lord" (hoc tantum facito Domino) adds "for the Lord" and "alone" where the Hebrew reads "observe to do all the word."
notes.13:6: Latin "fictor somniorum" ("fabricator of dreams") replaces the neutral "somniator" ("dreamer") of 13:4, emphasizing deliberate deceit.
notes.13:14: Latin "filii Belial" ("sons of Belial") renders the Hebrew idiom for worthless or wicked people using the personal-name form Belial.
notes.13:18: Latin "anathemate" ("accursed thing") translates Hebrew herem, referring to anything irrevocably devoted to God for total destruction under the ban.
notes.14:1: Latin uses the imperative "estote" ("Be sons") where the Hebrew and Septuagint have a declarative statement ("You are sons").
notes.14:5: The Vulgate follows the Septuagint's Greek zoological terms here, rendering the final five clean wild animals as wild ox (bubalum), goat-stag (tragelaphum), white-rumped antelope (pygargum), oryx (orygem), and giraffe (camelopardalum).
notes.14:13: Latin "ixion" is a Vulgate-distinct bird name (likely derived from a textual form of Greek iktinos, "kite") denoting a bird of prey; likewise "gryphem" ("griffin") in 14:12 follows the Septuagint term for a large carrion vulture such as the lammergeier.
notes.14:21: The Vulgate mentions only "the foreigner who is within your gates" (peregrino) for both giving and selling, whereas the Hebrew distinguishes the resident alien (to whom it may be given) from the foreigner (to whom it may be sold).
notes.15:5: The Vulgate places "He will bless you, as He has promised" at the close of verse 5 (and includes both "that He has commanded" and "that I command you today"), whereas the Hebrew places that blessing clause at the start of verse 6.
notes.15:10: Latin "nor shall you do anything craftily in relieving his needs" (nec ages quippiam callide in ejus necessitatibus sublevandis) is distinctly Vulgate; the Hebrew reads "nor shall your heart be grieved when you give to him."
notes.15:14: Latin "viaticum" literally means "provisions for the journey," giving a concrete sense to the Hebrew command to furnish the freed servant generously.
notes.15:18: Latin "according to the wages of a hired laborer" (juxta mercedem mercenarii) lacks the word "double" found in the Hebrew ("double the wages of a hired laborer"), and "Do not turn your eyes away from them" replaces the Hebrew idiom "Let it not seem hard in your eyes."
notes.16:1: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew month name Abib ("ears of grain") with the descriptive doublet novarum frugum, et verni primum temporis ("of new produce, and the first of the spring season").
notes.16:3: Latin in pavore ("in fear") is a distinctive Vulgate reading where the Hebrew text reads "in haste."
notes.16:11: Latin epulaberis ("you shall feast," also in v. 14) concretizes the Hebrew verb for rejoicing into a festive meal.
notes.16:20: Latin Juste quod justum est persequeris ("You shall justly pursue what is just") renders the emphatic Hebrew repetition ("Justice, justice") with an adverb and relative clause.
notes.16:21: Latin lucum ("grove") is the Vulgate's regular rendering of Hebrew Asherah; likewise statuam ("statue") in v. 22 renders the Hebrew sacred pillar.
notes.17:5: The Vulgate reads plural virum ac mulierem ("the man and the woman"), whereas the Hebrew text maintains the singular alternative ("that man or that woman").
notes.17:8: Latin lepram et lepram ("leprosy and leprosy") narrows the broader Hebrew phrase ("stroke and stroke" or "plague and plague") to skin disease.
notes.17:16: Latin equitatus numero sublevatus ("lifted up by the number of cavalry") is a distinctive Vulgate rendering where the Hebrew reads "in order to multiply horses."
notes.17:18: The Vulgate retains the Greek loanword Deuteronomium ("second law" or "copy of the law," whence the book's English title) for Hebrew mishneh ("copy"), and explicitly supplies accipiens exemplar ("receiving the copy").
notes.18:3: The Vulgate names only two sacrificial portions (armum ac ventriculum, "the shoulder and the stomach"), omitting the cheeks listed in the Hebrew text.
notes.18:8: Latin excepto eo, quod in urbe sua ex paterna ei successione debetur ("except for what is owed to him in his own city by paternal succession") clarifies an obscure Hebrew phrase commonly taken as proceeds from the sale of ancestral property.
notes.18:10: Latin lustret ... ducens per ignem ("purifies ... leading them through fire") frames the practice as pagan ritual purification, and observet somnia ("observes dreams") renders a debated Hebrew divination term.
notes.18:11: Latin pythones (translated "mediums") literally designates oracular spirits or persons possessed by a spirit of divination (cf. Acts 16:16).
notes.18:19: Latin ego ultor existam ("I Myself will be the avenger") is a vivid Vulgate rendering of the Hebrew idiom "I will require it of him."
notes.19:4: Vulgate adds legal evidentiary verbs in v. 4 (comprobatur, "is proved") and v. 6 (monstratur, "is shown"), and in v. 5 adds simpliciter ("simply," i.e., without guile), clarifying judicial proof of unintentional killing.
notes.19:6: Latin proximus ejus, cujus effusus est sanguis ("near relative of the one whose blood was shed"; similarly v. 12) renders Hebrew go'el haddam ("avenger of blood"); Vulgate also renders Hebrew "while his heart is hot" with dolore stimulatus ("goaded by grief").
notes.19:7: Vulgate specifies æqualis inter se spatii ("at equal distance from one another"), an explanatory detail not present in the Hebrew text (cf. also numerum duplicabis, "you shall double the number," in v. 9).
notes.19:21: Vulgate supplies the explicit verb exiges ("you shall exact"), whereas the Hebrew lists the five retaliatory phrases without a finite verb.
notes.20:4: Vulgate reads in medio vestri est ("is in your midst") and ut eruat vos de periculo ("to rescue you from danger"), where the Hebrew has "goes with you" and "to save you."
notes.20:6: Vulgate expands the Hebrew reference to releasing a vineyard's fruit for common use (cf. Lev 19:23-25) with de qua vesci omnibus liceat ("from which all are permitted to eat") and renders the final clause idiomatically as ejus fungatur officio ("perform his duty").
notes.20:9: Vulgate reads unusquisque suos ad bellandum cuneos præparabit ("each one shall prepare his own battle formations for fighting"), using the Roman military term cuneos, whereas the Hebrew states that commanders of armies shall be appointed at the head of the people.
notes.20:19: Where the Hebrew contains a famously disputed clause often read as a rhetorical question ("for is the tree of the field a man...?"), Vulgate renders it as a clear statement, quoniam lignum est, et non homo ("for it is a tree, and not a man"), and adds nec potest bellantium contra te augere numerum ("nor can it increase the number of those fighting against you").
notes.21:4: Vulgate renders Hebrew nachal eitan ("perennial wadi/stream") as vallem asperam atque saxosam ("a rough and rocky valley") and translates the ritual killing of the heifer as cædent ... cervices ("cut the neck"), rather than breaking its neck.
notes.21:5: Vulgate reads omne negotium, et quidquid mundum, vel immundum est ("every matter and whatever is clean or unclean"), interpreting Hebrew nega ("assault/plague") in its Levitical purity sense rather than as physical assault.
notes.21:6: Vulgate construes the elders as coming ad interfectum ("to the one who was killed"), whereas the Hebrew describes them as the elders of the city nearest to the dead man.
notes.21:20: Vulgate renders the two Hebrew epithets ("a glutton and a drunkard") with three classical Latin terms for dissipation: comessationibus ("carousing"), luxuriæ ("debauchery"), and conviviis ("banquets").
notes.21:22: Vulgate uses the Roman execution term in patibulo ("on a gibbet") in v. 22 and in ligno ("on the wood," corresponding to Hebrew ets / Greek xylon, "tree/wood") in v. 23, alongside the passive sepelietur ("shall be buried") and explicit maledictus a Deo ("cursed by God").
notes.22:9: Latin sanctificentur ('be sanctified') literally renders the Hebrew idiom for produce forfeited or consecrated to the sanctuary because of unlawful mixing.
notes.22:22: The Vulgate supplies the explanatory phrase id est, adulter et adultera ('that is, the adulterer and the adulteress'), whereas the Hebrew reads 'the man who lay with the woman and the woman.'
notes.22:26: Distinctively in the Vulgate, the attacker in the comparison is called a latro ('robber') rising against fratrem suum ('his brother'), where the Hebrew has 'a man' rising against 'his neighbor.'
notes.22:28: The Vulgate specifies et res ad judicium venerit ('and the matter comes to judgment'), where the Hebrew reads simply 'and they are found.'
notes.23:1: In the Latin, as in the Hebrew text, chapter 23 begins with this verse.
notes.23:2: The Clementine Vulgate prints intravit (literally perfect tense), an orthographic b/v variant for future intrabit ('shall enter'), and explicitly adds eunuchus ('eunuch') with attritis vel amputatis ('crushed or amputated').
notes.23:3: The Vulgate retains the Hebrew loanword mamzer and supplies the explanatory gloss hoc est, de scorto natus ('that is, one born of a prostitute'); ecclesiam ('assembly') renders the Septuagint term for the covenant congregation.
notes.23:15: The Clementine Vulgate reads quo revelatus es ('where you uncovered yourself'), a well-known variant for quo relevatus es ('that of which you were relieved,' referring to bodily waste).
notes.23:25: The Vulgate adds et manu conteres ('and rub them with your hand'), which is absent from the Hebrew text and echoes the wording of Luke 6:1.
notes.24:1: The Vulgate makes verse 1 a complete conditional sentence with main future verbs ("he shall write... place... and send her away"), whereas the Hebrew treats verses 1-3 as a single subordinate condition leading to the prohibition in verse 4.
notes.24:4: The Vulgate literally reads "and has become abominable before the Lord," making the wife the subject, whereas the Hebrew refers to the act of taking her back as an abomination.
notes.24:5: Latin laetetur cum uxore sua ("may rejoice with his wife") uses an intransitive verb, whereas the Hebrew reads "make his wife glad."
notes.24:8: The Vulgate reads ne incurras plagam leprae ("so that you do not incur the plague of leprosy"), framing the caution as avoiding infection rather than strictly observing rules during an outbreak as in the Hebrew.
notes.25:1: Latin justitiae palmam dabunt ("they shall give the palm of righteousness") uses a classical Roman victory metaphor to render the Hebrew "acquit the righteous."
notes.25:3: Latin foede laceratus... abeat ("depart shamefully torn") emphasizes physical laceration, whereas the Hebrew focuses on the brother being degraded in one's eyes.
notes.25:4: The Vulgate expands on the Hebrew ("while it is treading") by adding in area fruges tuas ("your produce on the threshing floor") and literally renders the verb as ligabis os ("bind the mouth").
notes.25:16: The Clementine Vulgate reads Dominus tuus ("your Lord"), without Deus ("God") as in the Hebrew text.
notes.26:5: Latin Syrus persequebatur patrem meum ("A Syrian was persecuting my father") reflects an ancient interpretive tradition referring to Laban pursuing Jacob, whereas the Hebrew reads "A wandering (or perishing) Aramean was my father."
notes.26:10: Latin adorato Domino Deo tuo is an ablative absolute ("having worshiped the Lord your God") leading syntactically into the verb of verse 11, where the Clementine Vulgate also retains a resumptive Et ("then").
notes.26:14: Latin in re funebri ("on a funeral matter") specifies funerary expenditure where the Hebrew reads "to the dead."
notes.26:17: Both here and in verse 18, the Vulgate translates the rare Hebrew verb ("declared/avouched") as elegisti and elegit ("have chosen" / "has chosen").
notes.26:19: The Vulgate adds the possessive suam ("for His praise, name, and glory"), directing the three terms explicitly to God rather than to Israel.
notes.27:3: The Vulgate reads 'sicut juravit patribus tuis' ("just as He swore to your fathers"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "just as the Lord, the God of your fathers, promised you."
notes.27:6: The Vulgate attaches 'et de saxis informibus et impolitis' ("and of unshaped and unpolished rocks") directly to the altar-building clause of verse 5 (which reads "that iron has not touched"), rather than repeating "you shall build the altar of the Lord your God" as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.27:7: The Vulgate reads 'et epulaberis' ("and you will feast"), highlighting the sacred banquet, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "and you shall rejoice."
notes.27:20: The Vulgate reads 'et revelat operimentum lectuli ejus' ("and uncovers the covering of his bed"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "because he has uncovered the skirt of his father."
notes.27:26: The Vulgate reads 'non permanet in sermonibus legis hujus, nec eos opere perficit' ("does not remain in the words of this law, and does not fulfill them in deed"), aligning with the Septuagint and Galatians 3:10 rather than the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "does not uphold the words of this law to do them."
notes.28:5: The Vulgate reads horrea tua ('your granaries', singular horreum in v. 17) and reliquiæ tuæ ('your remnants'), where the Hebrew has 'your basket' and 'your kneading trough' (taken by both the Septuagint and Vulgate from the related root meaning 'to remain').
notes.28:20: The Vulgate reads famem et esuriem ('famine and hunger') where the Hebrew has 'curse and confusion/panic'; the closing words reliquisti me ('you have forsaken Me') shift abruptly into the divine first person.
notes.28:21: From v. 21 through v. 35 the Vulgate shifts from the future indicative of vv. 1-20 to the optative/jussive present subjunctive (Adjungat, Percutiat, Sit, etc.), translated 'May...' to preserve the imprecatory curse mood of the Latin.
notes.28:22: The Vulgate renders these afflictions distinctively as egestate ('destitution'), frigore ('cold'), and aëre corrupto ('corrupted air') where the Hebrew has 'consumption', 'inflammation', and 'blight', and uses singular persequatur ('may He pursue you') with the Lord as subject.
notes.28:27: The Vulgate gives an explicit anatomical periphrasis, partem corporis, per quam stercora egeruntur ('the part of the body through which excrement is discharged'), for the Hebrew term meaning 'tumors' or 'hemorrhoids.'
notes.28:42: The Vulgate reads rubigo ('mildew', matching rubigine in v. 22), whereas the Hebrew term denotes a species of locust or whirring insect.
notes.28:54: The Vulgate mentions only the man's brother and wife, omitting the third phrase found in the Hebrew ('and the rest of his children whom he has left').
notes.28:57: The Clementine Vulgate has the plural verb Comedent ('they will eat') rather than the Hebrew singular ('she will eat').
notes.28:68: The Vulgate uses third-person dixit ('He told', referring to the Lord) and passive venderis ('you will be sold'), where the Hebrew has first-person 'I said to you' and reflexive 'you will offer yourselves for sale'.
notes.28:69: As in the Hebrew text, this summary verse concludes chapter 28 in the Latin (28:69).
notes.29:4: The Vulgate reads third-person Adduxit ('He led,' referring back to the Lord in 29:3) before shifting to first-person 'I am the Lord your God' in 29:5, whereas the Hebrew has first-person ('I led') in both verses.
notes.29:10: The Vulgate reads exceptis lignorum caesoribus, et his qui comportant aquas ('except the cutters of wood and those who carry water'), taking the Hebrew preposition exclusively rather than inclusively ('from your woodcutter to your water-drawer').
notes.29:14: The Vulgate compresses the longer Hebrew wording ('both with him who stands here with us today before the Lord our God and with him who is not here with us today') into the concise phrase sed cunctis praesentibus et absentibus ('but with all who are present and absent').
notes.29:18: The proverbial Vulgate clause et absumat ebria sitientem ('and the drunken one may consume the thirsty one') literally preserves the feminine adjectives of a notoriously difficult Hebrew expression, generally taken to signify sweeping away saturated and dry alike in collective ruin.
notes.29:25: The Vulgate uses a passive construction, et quibus non fuerant attributi ('and to whom they had not been assigned,' i.e., Israel to those gods), reversing the direction of the Hebrew ('whom He had not allotted to them').
notes.30:1: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew idiom 'bring back to your heart' explicitly as ductus poenitudine cordis tui ('led by repentance of your heart') and joins 'blessing' and 'curse' with sive ('or').
notes.30:4: The Latin ad cardines caeli literally refers to the 'hinges' or 'poles of heaven,' Jerome's poetic expression for the farthest ends of the sky.
notes.30:13: The Vulgate adds ut causeris ('so that you might make excuses') before 'and say,' and expands the end of the clause to ut possimus audire et facere quod praeceptum est ('so that we may be able to hear and do what has been commanded').
notes.30:16: Unlike the Hebrew ('in that I command you today to love...'), the Vulgate omits 'in that I command you today' and connects verse 16 directly to verse 15 as a purpose clause (ut diligas, 'so that you may love').
notes.31:6: The Vulgate uses the title ductor ("leader") here and in verse 8, rendering distinct Hebrew phrases ("goes with you" in v. 6 and "goes before you" in v. 8) with one consistent term.
notes.31:7: Latin reads "you will bring this people in" (introduces, agreeing with the Septuagint against the Hebrew "go with") and "divide it by lot" (sorte divides), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "cause them to inherit it."
notes.31:12: Whereas the Hebrew begins verse 12 with a new imperative ("Assemble the people"), the Vulgate continues the sentence from verse 11 with a coordinated ablative absolute ("and with all the people gathered together as one").
notes.31:17: The Vulgate turns the Hebrew rhetorical question ("Is it not because my God is not in my midst...?") into a direct affirmative statement ("Truly, because God is not with me..."), and reads "all evils" (omnia mala) rather than "many evils" (contrast v. 21).
notes.31:28: Latin renders the Hebrew term for tribal officers/officials (shoterim) as doctores ("teachers"), reflecting a traditional view of these leaders as instructors in the law; the Vulgate also omits "as witnesses" with "call upon heaven and earth."
notes.32:4: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew divine title "the Rock" as "God" (Dei, and similarly in vv. 15, 18, 30, 31, and 37), and reads plural "works" (opera) and "judgments" (judicia).
notes.32:15: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew poetic name for Israel, Jeshurun, as "the beloved" (dilectus), following the Septuagint tradition.
notes.32:24: Where the Hebrew text refers to burning plague or pestilence, the Vulgate renders "birds" (aves), picturing birds of prey devouring the people with a most bitter bite.
notes.32:35: The Vulgate reads "I will repay in time, so that their foot may slip" (et ego retribuam in tempore, ut labatur pes eorum) and plural "times" (tempora), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "vengeance is Mine and recompense, for the time when their foot slips."
notes.32:49: The Vulgate incorporates Jerome's explanatory gloss "that is, the Crossing" (id est, transitum) for the Hebrew name Abarim; similarly in v. 51 the Latin translates Meribah as "the waters of Contradiction" (aquas contradictionis).
notes.33:5: Latin rectissimum ("the most upright one"), repeated in 33:26, translates the poetic Hebrew title Jeshurun as a superlative adjective rather than a proper name; unlike the Hebrew past tense, the Vulgate also uses the future Erit ("There will be").
notes.33:10: Unlike the Hebrew ("They will teach Your ordinances to Jacob"), the Vulgate has no verb "teach," linking "Your judgments" and "Your law" to "observed" in v. 9 with vocatives to Jacob and Israel, and renders the Hebrew for "before You" / "to Your nostrils" literally as in furore tuo ("in Your wrath").
notes.33:17: Latin cornua rhinocerotis ("horns of a rhinoceros") is the Vulgate's distinctive rendering of the Hebrew re'em ("wild ox"), and ventilabit ("will scatter") literally means to winnow or toss into the air.
notes.33:21: Latin in parte sua doctor esset repositus ("in his portion the teacher was laid up") is the Vulgate's rendering of the difficult Hebrew clause about a commander's or lawgiver's portion, traditionally understood of Moses's burial in Gad's territory.
notes.33:28: Latin Oculus Jacob ("The eye of Jacob") translates Hebrew ayin literally as "eye" rather than "fountain," and caligabunt rore ("will grow dark with dew") reflects the Vulgate's reading of the Hebrew verb as clouding over or growing misty.
notes.34:2: Latin mare novissimum ("the farthest sea") translates the Hebrew expression for the Mediterranean ("the western/hinder sea") literally; similarly, australem partem in v. 3 renders the Negev descriptively as "the southern part."
notes.34:6: The Vulgate reads contra Phogor ("opposite Peor") without the prefix "Beth-" found in the Hebrew (Beth-peor).
notes.34:7: Latin nec dentes illius moti sunt ("nor were his teeth loosened") is a distinctive Vulgate rendering of the Hebrew clause "nor had his vigor fled."
